name: The Self-Serving Bias
statement: We take credit for our successes and blame our failures on everything else.
meaning: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute one's successes to internal factors like ability and effort, and one's failures to external factors like bad luck or unfair circumstances. Success flatters the self as earned, while failure is deflected onto conditions outside one's control. Its two faces are self-enhancement, taking credit for good outcomes, and self-protection, avoiding blame for bad ones, and together they cushion self-esteem.
mechanism: Two families of explanation compete and probably combine. A motivational account holds that the bias defends and enhances self-esteem, steering us to flattering conclusions. A cognitive account holds that it falls out of ordinary expectation: because we generally expect to succeed, we attribute expected outcomes to ourselves and unexpected ones to circumstance, with no ego motive required. The modern view treats these as intertwined, since motives shape what information we seek, notice, and scrutinise, so cognition and motivation work in tandem.

examples.text: A good grade is credited to being smart and studying hard, while a poor one is blamed on unfair questions or a bad teacher.
Athletes and fans credit victories to skill and effort but losses to referees, bad calls, or conditions, a pattern documented in sport.
Teams and groups attribute their own successes to internal virtues and their failures to outside forces, while reversing the pattern for rivals.

variants.name: Cultural moderation
variants.text: The bias is large in individualist Western samples but much weaker, sometimes absent or reversed toward self-effacement, in some East Asian and collectivist contexts.

variants.name: Reduced bias in depression
variants.text: Depressed and distressed individuals tend to show a weaker self-serving bias; the stronger claim that they see reality more accurately, depressive realism, is separately contested.

whyItMatters: It is a central mechanism by which people protect and enhance their self-worth, with consequences for relationships and workplaces, where each side may claim successes and deflect failures, fuelling conflict. It bears on motivation, feedback, and mental health, and it is a staple of attribution research, illuminating how our explanations of outcomes bend toward preserving a favourable image of ourselves.

working.text: notice when you credit good outcomes to yourself and bad ones to circumstance, and check whether the split is fair.
extend to others the situational explanations you reach for in your own failures, to reduce blame and conflict.
remember the bias varies with culture, age, and mood, so its strength is not fixed.

limits: The overall pattern is one of the most robust in social psychology at the aggregate level, but its causes and magnitude are qualified. The mechanism, motivational versus cognitive, remains debated, with the intertwined view an interpretive synthesis. The size is strongly moderated by culture, age, mood, and clinical status, being large in Western samples and small or absent in some collectivist ones. Notably, the influential Miller and Ross review was skeptical, finding solid evidence only for the self-enhancing half.
misreadings: The landmark Miller and Ross review did not establish the bias; it was critical, finding only weak support and arguing the success half may be non-motivational. It is not purely motivated ego-defence, since a cognitive, expectation-based account is a serious rival. It is not a fixed human universal, being strongly culturally moderated. And a reduced bias in depression is not the same as depressed people being more realistic, a separately disputed claim.
origin: Rooted in the attribution theory of Fritz Heider and Harold Kelley and studied intensively from the 1970s; the influential critical review is Dale Miller and Michael Ross's 1975 paper in Psychological Bulletin.

sources.text: Miller & Ross, "Self-Serving Biases in the Attribution of Causality: Fact or Fiction?," Psychological Bulletin 82 (1975): 213-225. — the critical review and the enhancement-versus-protection distinction.
Self-serving bias, Wikipedia. — the success-internal failure-external pattern, the motivational-cognitive debate, and cultural moderation.
